known_facts_book1: Is the black kitten, finished with its washing earlier in the afternoon, that unwinds Alice's ball of worsted over the hearth-rug.
Is charged with three faults: squeaking while Dinah washed its face, pulling Snowdrop away by the tail, and unwinding the worsted.
Is held up to the glass and threatened with Looking-glass House, and refuses to fold its arms like the Red Queen.
Never goes through the glass: it is on the hearth-rug when Alice wakes, purring.
Is set face to face with the Red Queen chessman at the end and looks a little ashamed of itself, so Alice concludes it was the Red Queen.

known_relations_book1.Alice: Her kitten, scolded, lectured and finally accused of having been the Red Queen.
known_relations_book1.Dinah: Its mother, who washes its face.
known_relations_book1.Snowdrop: The white kitten it pulled away by the tail.

not_in_this_book: Kitty appears in the Looking-glass world

known_facts_book1: Is the white kitten, having its face washed by the old cat for the last quarter of an hour and bearing it pretty well.
Had a saucer of milk put down before her, and was pulled away by the tail by the black kitten.
Is still patiently undergoing its toilet at the end of the book, when Alice calls her 'your White Majesty' and decides she was the White Queen.
Never speaks and never leaves the hearth-rug.

known_relations_book1.Alice: Her white kitten, addressed at the end as the White Queen.
known_relations_book1.Dinah: Its mother, still scrubbing it in the last chapter.
known_relations_book1.Kitty: The black kitten that pulled her away from the milk.

not_in_this_book: Snowdrop appears in the Looking-glass world

known_facts_book1: Is the old cat, mother of the two kittens, who washes their faces by holding them down by one ear and rubbing the wrong way from the nose.
Is reproached by Alice for not having taught the black kitten better manners.
Is still washing Snowdrop in the last chapter, and Alice tells her she is scrubbing a White Queen.
Never goes through the glass; Alice only wonders aloud whether Dinah turned into Humpty Dumpty, and says she is not sure.

known_relations_book1.Alice: Her cat, scolded at the start and questioned at the end.

known_facts_book1: Is a very old Frog sitting under a tree by the door lettered QUEEN ALICE, dressed in bright yellow with enormous boots on.
Speaks in a deep hoarse whisper Alice can scarcely hear, and drawls so slowly she almost stamps with irritation.
Asks which door, then what the door has been asking of, and tells Alice she shouldn't knock because it vexes it.
Kicks the door with one of his great feet and hobbles back to his tree, advising her to let it alone and it'll let her alone.

known_relations_book1.Alice: The only creature who answers her at the door of her own house, and refuses to open it.

not_in_this_book: the Frog opens the door for Alice
the Frog serves at the banquet

known_facts_book1: Exists only in the poem Alice reads by holding the looking-glass book up to a glass; it never appears in the story.
Is described with jaws that bite and claws that catch, and eyes of flame, coming whiffling through the tulgey wood and burbling as it came.
Is killed by an unnamed beamish boy with a vorpal blade, who leaves it dead and goes galumphing back with its head.
Its hard words are later glossed by Humpty Dumpty, who explains brillig, slithy, toves, gyre, gimble, wabe, mimsy, borogove and mome raths.
Alice's whole verdict on the poem is that somebody killed something, that's clear at any rate.

known_relations_book1.Alice: Reads about it; the two never meet.
known_relations_book1.Humpty Dumpty: Explains the vocabulary of the poem it lives in.

not_in_this_book: the Jabberwock guards the Eighth Square
the White Knight slew the Jabberwock

known_facts_book1: Is named in the 'Jabberwocky' poem as the frumious Bandersnatch, to be shunned along with the Jubjub bird.
Is used twice by the White King as a figure of speed: you might as well try to stop a Bandersnatch, and you might as well try to catch a Bandersnatch.
Never appears on the page and is never seen by anybody.

known_relations_book1.White King: Uses it as his comparison for a minute going by and for the White Queen running.

known_facts_book1: Speaks exactly once, saying it never saw anybody that looked stupider, so suddenly that Alice jumps.
Is told by the Tiger-lily to hold its tongue, since it keeps its head under the leaves and snores away there.
Says nothing else for the rest of the book.

known_relations_book1.Tiger-lily: Silences it immediately after its one remark.
known_relations_book1.Alice: The target of its single insult.

not_in_this_book: the Violet speaks with Alice at length

known_facts_book1: Speaks exactly one line, crying 'She's coming!' and saying it hears the Red Queen's footstep along the gravel-walk.
Is the flower that announces the Red Queen's arrival in the garden, and says nothing else.

known_relations_book1.Alice: Present for its one line; they never speak to each other.
